@SarthakGoswami I regularly follow Sunday Samachar and News Midweek, which is precisely why I was surprised not to see a detailed discussion on the Swatantra Bhardwaj bail controversy.

I genuinely believe this deserves an episode—not because one person receiving bail is itself proof of wrongdoing, but because the contrast in treatment across politically sensitive cases raises serious questions about due process, pre-trial incarceration and equality before law.

When someone receives judicial relief after a relatively short period in custody, while another accused person in a completely different case can remain incarcerated for years without the trial reaching its conclusion, surely this deserves scrutiny from independent journalists.

The question is not whether Bhardwaj should have been granted bail or whether Umar Khalid should be released. The question is whether our criminal-justice system applies the same constitutional principles—liberty, due process and equality before law—consistently, irrespective of political identity or influence.

If political connections can create even the perception that some people are able to navigate the system more easily than ordinary citizens, that perception itself is damaging to public trust.

And this is exactly where your journalism can add value.

You have the platform, the audience and, more importantly, the ability to examine uncomfortable questions that mainstream television often avoids.

Please consider covering this—not as a political argument for one side, but as an investigation into whether our justice system is truly delivering equal treatment under the law.

Because if the law is equal, journalism should have no hesitation in testing that equality against the facts.

In my hometown, sanitation workers clean the roads, dump the waste into the sewage right in front of us, monsoon comes, drains clog and roads flood. Then they clean the sewage, dump that sludge back onto the road, half of it washes right back in, and the rest gets picked up a week later. Then repeat. 🤦🏻

The bigger problem is that India has historically dumped sanitation work onto one community—Valmiki Samaj—and decided it's somehow “their work.” So we stigmatize the job, have a shortage of workers, overwork the ones we have, give them inadequate systems, and then blame them when the system fails.

In many Western countries, sanitation is simply a job. Here, we've turned it into a caste-assigned responsibility.

Until we stop looking down on sanitation work and start treating it as essential work that anyone can do with dignity, decent pay and proper infrastructure, we'll keep cleaning the same garbage twice and wondering why our cities are still filthy.

Vicious cycle, literally and socially. 😑

Meri bhi yehi story chal rahi hai filhal but mera loan education loan tha aur woh bhi sirf 4 lakh ka, aur maine apne pehle loan ke baad dusra loan nahi liya. Mere papa actually court mein case lad rahe the SBI ke against kyuki unhone interest rate bdha ke lagaya tha. Aur 1.75 lakh papa ne case hone se pehle bhar diye the, fir woh expire ho gaye, unfortunately, aur tab se bank wale besharmi se mere aur meri mummy ke peechhe padhe hue hai, jabki yeh saari baat unko bta chuke hai hum ki humko case ki details nahi pata woh papa hi deal karte the, aur main unemployed hun upar se mummy completely bedridden hai, but in sab se unko kya lena dena, unhone toh khud bol diya tha, infact judge ne bhi on record yeh bola ki kahi aur se loan utha lo ya udhaar le lo aur bank walo ke paise chukaao varna mujhe jail bhej denge aur humara ghar jo ek lauta asset hai usko auction se bech ke apne paise nikalwa lenge. Matlab ek banda inke paise jugaad karne ke chakkar mein kuch galat kadam utha le aur nahi toh jo ek le deke rehne ka jugaad hai maa-bete ke pass usko hi minimum rate pe bech ke unke sar ki chhat chheen lo.

Absolutely nothing.

Matlab ek banda inke paise jugaad karne ke chakkar mein kuch galat kadam utha le aur nahi toh jo ek le deke rehne ka jugaad hai maa-bete ke pass usko hi minimum rate pe bech ke unke sar ki chhat chheen lo. Absolutely nothing. The bank manager has bought the Judge (of which I was skeptical of initially, but over the time he made sure that I know that I have nowhere to escape until I pay each and everything) and he is hell bent on making the ends meet for the bank ofcourse, koi family jispe survival vaise hi bhaari padh raha hai usko beghar karke pura beggar hi bana do toh koi baat nahi, bas vasooli mein kami nahi aani chahiye kahi se bhi. By the way, humne yeh ek bhi baar nahi bola ki hum payment nahi denge ya de paayenge, humne sirf jo interest rate zabardasti ka lagaya hua hai woh maaf karne ke liye aur jo baaki ka amount pending hai usko pay karne ke liye apt time de taaki hum installations mein bhar sake, but nahi, unko pura ka pura chahiye woh bhi soot samet varna bhaad mein jaao unki bla se.

Maine abhi hi government exam ke liye Labour Law poora padha hai. Usme iska reason bhi diya hua hai. Jo factory worker ₹15,000/- se kam kama raha ho, usko ESI Act ki taraf se medical insurance milta hai, plus EPF Act ke chalte Provident Fund bhi collect hote rehta hai ₹1,250/- ka. Aur jo ₹15,000/- ke upar kama raha ho, woh yeh benefits claim nahi kar sakta, uske liye bas Retrenchment aur Compensation ka hi option hota hai.

It's not just students—even working professionals like us face pretty much the same issue in Noida. Rent for a basic 1 RK is around 10k, and once you add food and commute, it easily touches 20k. For an entry-level engineer in IT, that's sometimes 80%+ of their salary, and even for folks with close to 5 years of experience, it's a third of their pay. And what do you get for that? No exhaust, no balcony, no windows facing an open street for fresh air, no lift even if you're on the 5th floor or higher—it's so cramped that on weekends it honestly feels like living in a jail.

I genuinely don't get what the problem is with IT companies insisting people come to office, or even just hybrid - hybrid is a scam. Individuals would save money, and companies would save on infrastructure too. It's a win-win either way.

As I see it, I have also benefited from reservation, so I understand this issue from that perspective.
First, getting admission through reservation does not mean someone automatically gets a degree. You still have to complete the course, clear the required examinations, and fulfil the university’s academic requirements to receive the degree. The qualification is ultimately awarded only after meeting those requirements.
Second, I think we should distinguish between reservation and professional competence. If someone enters a profession through a reserved seat but later performs poorly or lacks the required skills, the solution should be stronger training, examinations, supervision and accountability—not simply blaming the reservation system.
For example, a CHO is not the same as a medical doctor. The important question should be whether the person has completed the prescribed training and is competent to perform the responsibilities assigned to that position.
And regarding the argument that “reserved-category candidates have no merit,” that is too broad a generalisation. There are competent and incompetent people in every category. If someone gets a job through corruption, influence or money and then performs poorly, that is a problem of selection and accountability, not something that can fairly be attributed to an entire reserved community.
If the real concern is professionalism, then we should demand the same thing from everyone: proper qualification, proper training, transparent selection, periodic evaluation and strict accountability. Judge the individual’s competence—not their caste or the category through which they entered.

Subject: Story Pitch: Condition of Medical Students & Junior Doctors in Madhya Pradesh (MGM Medical College, Indore)

Dear Mr. Sarthak Goswami,

I hope this email finds you well.

I am writing to bring to your attention a matter of significant public interest concerning the condition of medical students and junior doctors across Madhya Pradesh, and to request that your desk consider covering it.

I am currently a first-year MBBS student at MGM Medical College, Indore, which is one of the highest-ranked medical colleges in the state. Based on my own experience and documentary evidence, I would like to highlight the following issues:

1. 'Vachan Patra' (Proforma-9) — Coerced Undertaking Silencing Students: As a precondition for admission, every MBBS/BDS student in Madhya Pradesh is forced to sign a notarized affidavit on Rs. 200 stamp paper stating that they are satisfied with the government-fixed course fee and monthly stipend, will never remain absent without authorization, and will never participate in any strike — under any circumstance. The document explicitly warns that if a student is found violating this clause, their admission will be cancelled under Rule 17(3) of the MP Medical Education Admission Rules, 2018. In effect, an 18-year-old is made to sign away their constitutional right to protest and their right to collectively bargain for fair stipends, under direct threat of losing their medical seat — before they have even attended their first class. Subject: Story Pitch: Condition of Medical Students & Junior Doctors in Madhya Pradesh (MGM Medical College, Indore)

Dear Mr. Sarthak Goswami,

I hope this email finds you well.

I am writing to bring to your attention a matter of significant public interest concerning the condition of medical students and junior doctors across Madhya Pradesh, and to request that your desk consider covering it.

I am currently a first-year MBBS student at MGM Medical College, Indore, which is one of the highest-ranked medical colleges in the state. Based on my own experience and documentary evidence, I would like to highlight the following issues:

1. 'Vachan Patra' (Proforma-9) — Coerced Undertaking Silencing Students: As a precondition for admission, every MBBS/BDS student in Madhya Pradesh is forced to sign a notarized affidavit on Rs. 200 stamp paper stating that they are satisfied with the government-fixed course fee and monthly stipend, will never remain absent without authorization, and will never participate in any strike — under any circumstance. The document explicitly warns that if a student is found violating this clause, their admission will be cancelled under Rule 17(3) of the MP Medical Education Admission Rules, 2018. In effect, an 18-year-old is made to sign away their constitutional right to protest and their right to collectively bargain for fair stipends, under direct threat of losing their medical seat — before they have even attended their first class. I have enclosed a copy of this affidavit for your reference.

2. RURAL SERVICE BOND — One-Year Bonded Labour Clause: A separate undertaking,   RURAL SERVICE BOND  , effectively binds students/interns to a designated hospital or institution for a period of one year, denying them the freedom to choose a hospital or institution offering better pay, training, or working conditions during that period. This amounts to a de facto bonded-labour arrangement, forcing young doctors into low-paid or exploitative postings with no contractual leverage or exit option, even when better-compensated opportunities are available elsewhere.

3. Protest at GMC Bhopal: Junior doctors protesting at Gandhi Medical College (GMC), Bhopal were subjected to a lathi charge and water cannons by the police, raising serious concerns about how legitimate grievances of medical professionals are being handled by the administration — grievances that students are, on paper, not even permitted to raise.

4. Condition of Junior Doctors and Interns: Junior doctors and interns across various government hospitals in Madhya Pradesh continue to work under difficult conditions, including long duty hours, inadequate stipends, and insufficient institutional support.

5. Hostel Conditions at Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Block-2, MGMC Indore: The hostel block allotted to first-year MBBS students is reportedly in poor condition, raising safety and living-standard concerns — especially significant in light of the recent Satya Niketan, Delhi incident, which has brought student housing safety into national focus.

Taken together, these five issues point to a systemic pattern: medical students and junior doctors in Madhya Pradesh are being denied basic rights of protest, mobility, and dignified living conditions, often under the threat of losing their admission or career. I believe this story deserves wider attention, as it directly concerns the wellbeing, rights, and safety of the people who form the backbone of our healthcare system. I would be happy to share further documentation, photographs, or put you in touch with fellow students and junior doctors willing to speak on record or on condition of anonymity.

Please let me know if you would like to discuss this further or require any additional information.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Warm regards,
[PLS DONT DISCLOSE MY NAME
MBBS Student, MGM Medical College, Indore

Enclosures: Vachan Patra (Proforma-9) — copy attached

Sarthak Bhai, I genuinely want to understand your position here, because I feel there are some serious inconsistencies in the way you are looking at these protests.

First, please watch your own Jharkhand video, where you yourself acknowledged that thousands of people were coming and going, and in such a massive crowd, it is impossible to know exactly who was raising which slogan. If random slogans can be dismissed as the actions of individuals in one protest, then how can you use particular slogans in another protest to characterize the entire movement as organized or ideological? Isn’t that a double standard?

The comparison people in this de-reservation protest are making with CJP also needs to be understood properly. They are comparing themselves with CJP because, as they understand it, CJP had permission to conduct its protest at that particular place, whereas these protesters were not initially even given permission to protest there. Yes, permission was later granted for a protest at Ramlila Maidan, but that does not automatically make the original treatment of their protest fair.

And honestly, before judging any protest, I think we should actually read their demands and understand what they are asking for instead of simply labeling the entire movement.

One of the demands I personally find worth discussing is the idea that reservation should perhaps be given to a family only once, rather than continuing indefinitely across generations within the same family. Another version of the demand is that reservation should continue until someone from that family achieves a certain level of economic and social stability and moves above the genuinely disadvantaged category.

Whether we agree with this proposal or not, it deserves an actual discussion.

The same logic should apply when we talk about EWS. If EWS reservation is intended for economically weaker sections, then shouldn’t its benefits primarily reach people who are genuinely economically disadvantaged?

People also ask a very basic question: what about a genuinely poor person from a community that does not receive caste-based reservation? Has that person done something wrong simply because they were born into a particular community?

At the same time, if someone who is already financially well-off manages to obtain a fraudulent certificate and takes benefits intended for genuinely disadvantaged people, that is obviously a serious problem too.

I know these issues are not perfectly interconnected, but they are all part of the larger conversation about how reservation should work, who should qualify, and how we can ensure that benefits actually reach the people who need them.

I am not saying there is a simple answer to all of this. My point is that we should discuss reservation, protests, eligibility, economic disadvantage, misuse of certificates, representation and equality using the same standard for everyone.

And coming back to the original question: are you actually against reservation, or are you against certain aspects of the current reservation system? Because those are two very different positions.

And finally, let’s take the competence argument seriously. Suppose a student scores -40 marks in an examination and eventually becomes a doctor because of reservation. Would you personally be comfortable getting a major operation done by that person?

If the answer is no, then shouldn’t we honestly discuss where we draw the line between social justice, representation, economic disadvantage and professional competence?

The point isn’t to attack anyone. The point is to have a consistent conversation where the same standards are applied to everyone.

जब लोग ब्राह्मण या अन्य जातियों में शादी को लेकर फालतू का विवाद खड़ा करते हैं, तो वे ज़मीनी हकीकत भूल जाते हैं। भारत में ब्राह्मण और राजपूतों की आबादी उतनी है ही नहीं, जितनी SC, ST या मुस्लिम आबादी है। गणित के हिसाब से देखें तो लड़कियाँ पूरी ही नहीं पड़ेंगी। तो फिर इस फ़साद का क्या मतलब है? जब लड़के-लड़की को एक-दूसरे को चुनना है, तो अंतरजातीय विवाह होने दीजिए, उनकी पसंद को मायने रखने दीजिए।

हमेशा आरक्षण हटाने का शोर तो मचता है, लेकिन जातिवाद खत्म करने की बात कोई नहीं करता। याद रखिए, जिस दिन जाति खत्म होगी, आरक्षण और जातिवाद अपने-आप खत्म हो जाएगा। और इसे बदलने का सबसे तेज़ रास्ता इंटरकास्ट मैरिज है। अगर हम इसे अपनाएं, तो 10 साल में 40% जातिवाद खत्म हो सकता है, और अगले 30 से 40 साल में पूरा समाज एक समान हो सकता है।

raw_text:
Hello Bhaiya and everyone,
Here's what I feel about being in India and being categorised as Schedule Caste, I belong from Raipur, Chhattisgarh, recently we were looking for an apartment to rent while our home was renovated, the very first question which the landlords and landladies would ask was, "Aapki Jaati kya hoti hai, kisme aate hai aap?" Well I'm 22 now and used to such kind of questions, and the moment we said, Schedule Caste - Satnami, they would politely deny us from entering their property.
Another incident is that, I went to a really good school of Chhattisgarh, I mean top 2nd, their we were only 3 students from Sc,Stand Obc and rest all of them were from General category and the moment our class teacher announced that for the registration in the CBSE board examination of 12th Standard we require our Caste Certificate and mind you that announcements with our names that these 3 students need to bring their caste certificates made the entire class look at us like we are from some different planet and I felt like dying at that moment. I somehow belong to a good background where my father is an engineer because of reservation, but my grandfather was illiterate, my great grandfather was also illiterate and so on, where as there are my uppered class friends whose parents, grandparents, great grandparents were somehow very educated and had a well paid job. Coming to the other incident, when I visited my doc for my regular checkup he asked me, "Are you also a part of the drama going on at Jantar Mantar" I said yes, and then he said  "saare neele kabutar ikkathhe hai wahan", people talk about that creamy layer should be introduced in SC-Sts I just have one question, despite of belonging from a good and stable economic background I feel the discrimination. The moment I entered LSR with a reserved seat, people there made fun of me, also with the same reservation of EWS people don't have a problem...so I don't think in anywhich way castism has decreased or will be out of our society even in future because the way through which it was performed has changed but castism still exists.

There were 3 girls in the metro discussing how badly SC-STs stink and how dark their skin colour is?

Also a question to everyone who is reading this, I don't see a single millionaire from SC-Sts, I can't find the name tags of the banglows in south Delhi having the titles of SC-Sts, I can't find a general category sewage worker, I can't see any general category person cleaning that man hole for food. If people can have purity hawans after the visit of Kharge ji, if people can make fun of our Tribal President and who am I or the other SC-Sts personnel to not face castism.
Reservation gave my father education, reservation gave me a place at LSR, it gave me an opportunity, wealth does not always define your social dignity.

Thankfully, my family runs on a parallel universe 😂🙂. My elder sister doesn’t even know how to cook, while I can cook mostly Everything, and whenever my family goes out, I’m usually the one who cooks, with my sister helping me. I also help my mom with household chores.

In our family, everyone washes their own clothes too, and during festivals, the household responsibilities are divided among everyone. No work is considered “Only for Women” or “Only for Men.”

So honestly, I sometimes feel like my family has stepped a little outside the traditional Patriarchal Mindset. 😂

And I have absolutely no shame in saying that. I’m actually proud of it. These aren’t “just household chores” they’ve taught me how to take care of myself, manage a home, and live independently.

Education and awareness are important, but knowing how to take care of yourself and your home is also a real life skill. Wherever I go in life, I know I can manage on my own 🗿

I understand the historical reasons behind caste based reservation, but honestly, in my friend circle, no one really had this idea of casteism until competitive exams came into the picture. If someone from a reserved category is in the same financial bracket as me...(or even better off)..then isn’t it a form of discrimination towards me that I have to score more for the same seat just because I was born into the general category? Being born in the general category doesn’t automatically mean I’m rich or privileged.
I’m preparing for CAT right now, and even as an EWS student, I’m still supposed to pay the same fees as a gen student. So what exactly is the point of the “economically weaker” category if there isn’t a meaningful difference in financial assistance? I’m not saying caste based discrimination doesn’t exist or that historical disadvantages don’t matter. But shouldn’t the system focus more on someone’s actual financial and social circumstances rather than assuming privilege based on the category they were born into?

Bro, regarding what you're saying about the scam—one house being used for photos of 3,000 people—something similar happens in Bihar too.

For example, under the government toilet (Swachh Bharat) scheme in many villages, only one person actually builds a toilet. After that, people from the entire village stand in front of the same toilet one by one and get their photos clicked as if each of them has built one. The official who comes for verification often takes a cut. Suppose the government releases ₹10,000; the verifier may keep around ₹5,000 and give the remaining amount to the beneficiary.

So I don't think it's entirely a government scam. During audits, officials often don't verify the actual ground reality. The bigger issue is that many local people themselves don't want genuine development. Even today, in my village, many people still go to the roadside instead of using toilets, and they spend the government money on other personal needs.

The same thing happens with government housing schemes. The government allocates money for houses, but only one house gets built. Then people from the entire village use that same house for photos to claim benefits. Out of ₹100,000, the verification official may take ₹40,000–₹50,000, and the rest is shared.

This has been happening in many rural areas of Bihar. If possible, you should also cover this aspect on the ground. The government may be providing the funds, but if local people and corrupt officials misuse the schemes, real development never happens. Then, when the government doesn't provide benefits, people blame the government, and when it does, some people still don't want actual development and continue living in mud houses while misusing the funds.

Sarthak bhai, I still didn't see any words in this about the students who preferred violence. If police are taking action against those, what's the problem with it? If I throw stones at someone in protest, then whoever suffered loss because of me can ask the police to detain me. Then what is wrong with police? Then my friends, who are seeing me detained, are now throwing stones at police; this is how it happened. How will you address this situation?

And CJP is asking them bluntly to release all protestors now. Why should the police release me if I started throwing stones?

How long will you keep on asking for resignations after mistakes are done and damage is caused?

In the past, were we blaming Allu Arjun, Vijay Thalapathy, RCB and many other actors for being the reason for the stampede due to improper management of the crowd?

Did you ask CJP leaders what was done for crowd management? What was done for managing students in protest?

For taking accountability of a decision by minister, how long will it be right to keep protesting on the issues and asking for resignations for ministers rather than making them accept and demand appropriate outcomes?

Was actually CJP successful in this protest? Or can a senior and expert leader, like Sonum Sir, help to get an outcome out of it?

Only because cockroaches can overcome nuclear radiation should we all become cockroaches and live happy lives to feel safe from radiation fear? Or avoid exposure to nuclear radiation?

Should the CJP need a senior and responsible leader who can think of managing both the protest's core topic and the crowd during a protest?

The protest was against Education Minister Pradhan, sir. Then why were there chants over Modi in protest, but not just chants, but like he was some street vendor and not the PM of India?

Management and conveyance issue, If the protest was for NEET paper leaks, why were other people on stage chanting/chit-chatting over 'Naame Rahe Allah' (no offence with religion and poem/song, but was that necessary?) & 'Sita ke pati to Nita ke pati'?

He had implemented some development and brought in accountability by punishing the accused? Can he skip resignation and  work on improving crime conviction rate upto 100% (example: If 4 cases occur, then all the 4 accused are being punished with no chance of bail/early leave.) Can this actually help over resignation?

Should there be any private body like the CJP over it, don't just start RESIGNATION RESIGNATION, but work on demanding the correct outcome for goodwill, considering the future?

(My example) I'm working as a senior engineer team lead now and completed 5 years in the same company this year, having started as a civil engineer in 2021. Now, in 2021 during my probation, I made several mistakes unknowingly or mistakenly. But the company didn't fire me. They worked on my mistakes because they knew the appropriate solutions for my problems and also helped me avoid mistakes. It's 2026, here now. I'm making standards with my company so new members of my team don't make the same mistakes I did at first.
Would this be the best case where the company asked me to resign in my 1st year?

There are so many questions, but how are we going about the few above? No one, not even them, is speaking about it?
